statement: In children born in Sweden from 1950 to 1993 and adopted within Sweden, both what was passed on from their biological parents and features of the adoptive home they grew up in were associated with a later register record of drug problems; the study estimated no heritability percentage. Of 18,115 adoptees followed in national registers to 2009 (a record meant a diagnosis of a drug use disorder or drug psychosis in hospital, outpatient, primary-care or death records, a drug-related conviction, or long-term high-volume collection of prescribed sedatives or opioids; alcohol and tobacco excluded; the study calls this 'drug abuse'), 4.5% had a record, against 2.9% of everyone born in Sweden in the same years. Adoptees whose biological parent had a record, though they were not raised by that parent, had one in 8.6% of cases against 4.2% when neither biological parent had (odds ratio 2.09, 95% CI 1.66 to 2.62), and in 11.9% when both had; records were also shared with biological siblings raised apart (full siblings, odds ratio 1.84, 1.28 to 2.64; half siblings, 1.41, 1.19 to 1.67). In the adoptive home, records were shared with adoptive siblings, who had no genes in common with the adoptee: 6.2% of the adoptive siblings of adoptees with a record had one, against 3.2% of the adoptive siblings of adoptees without (odds ratio 1.95, 1.43 to 2.65), and the adoptive mother's divorce and an adoptive parent's death were also associated with a record; adoptees raised by an adoptive parent with a record had one in 6.8% of cases against 4.5%, an imprecise estimate that included no difference (1.55, 0.86 to 2.80), with only 1.0% of adoptive parents affected. On the scale of absolute risk, an adverse adoptive home added more risk for adoptees whose biological relatives' records put them at higher risk, an interaction the paper does not report on the odds scale (Kendler et al., 2012). An adoption study separates the family that passes on genes from the family that raises a child, but what passes from biological parents includes the pregnancy, care before placement (up to about 3 in 10 adoptees may have joined their adoptive family after age 5) and how agencies matched children to homes, as well as genes; the authors' argument against effects in the womb rests on 9.9% with an affected biological father against 8.2% with an affected mother, overlapping intervals without a test. As summarized, without figures, by a narrative review, twin studies find that genes and both shared and individual environment influence whether people start using tobacco, alcohol or cannabis, that genes matter more for regular use and dependence, and that the shared family environment is no longer detectable for regular use or dependence in adulthood though it is in adolescence (the adoptive-sibling association above, if it reflects the shared home, does not fit this summary well); single genetic variants have small effects that replicate poorly, scores combining many variants explained less than 1% of the variation in alcohol dependence, and the size of genetic influence has been reported to differ between environments (Prom-Wormley et al., 2017, second-hand). A heritability, where one is given, describes how much of the differences between people in one population at one time go with differences in their genes; it is not the share of any one person's risk that comes from genes (the editors' explanation; Visscher et al., 2008, on what heritability means, is not yet read). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: How much do genes and family shape drug problems? Both matter, in a large Swedish study of adopted children. Children whose birth parent had a drug problem in official records had one themselves about twice as often (about 9 in 100, against 4 in 100 when neither birth parent did), even though other parents raised them. Drug problems were also shared within adoptive families, between children not related by birth: when an adopted child had one, about 6 in 100 of their adoptive brothers and sisters did too, against 3 in 100 when the adopted child did not. Divorce or a parent's death in the adoptive family also went with more drug problems. The study did not work out a percentage due to genes, and what comes from birth parents also includes the pregnancy and the time before adoption. A percentage due to genes, where studies give one, describes differences between people in one place and time; it does not say how much of one person's risk comes from genes.
population: Children born in Sweden 1950–1993 and adopted within Sweden by non-relatives, living with their adoptive parents by age 10 (18,115 adoptees; national registers to 2009); twin studies summarized without figures by a narrative review
exposure: A register record of drug problems in biological parents or in biological siblings not raised with the adoptee (what passes from biological relatives: genes, pregnancy, care before placement), and in adoptive siblings or parents, or disruption of the adoptive home (the rearing environment)
comparator: Adoptees whose biological, or adoptive, relatives had no such record
outcome: A register record of drug problems (the study's 'drug abuse': drug use disorder or drug psychosis diagnoses, drug-related convictions or long-term high-volume collection of prescribed sedatives or opioids; alcohol and tobacco excluded)
magnitude: Kendler et al. (2012): adoptees with a record 4.5% (95% CI 4.2–4.8; 820 people) vs 2.9% nationally for the same birth years. Biological parent with vs without a record 8.6% vs 4.2%, OR 2.09 (1.66–2.62); none, one or both biological parents 4.2%, 8.2%, 11.9%; biological father 9.9% (7.2–12.1), mother 8.2% (6.3–10.5). Biological full siblings raised apart, record in 10.7% of the full siblings of adoptees with a record vs 6.1% of those of adoptees without, OR 1.84 (1.28–2.64); half siblings 7.4% vs 5.3%, OR 1.41 (1.19–1.67). Adoptive siblings of adoptees with vs without a record 6.2% vs 3.2%, OR 1.95 (1.43–2.65); adoptees raised by an adoptive parent with vs without a record 6.8% vs 4.5%, OR 1.55 (0.86–2.80). Multivariable: adoptive mother's divorce OR 1.31 (1.03–1.68), adoptive parent's death 1.37 (1.08–1.73). Interaction on the probability scale 0.0005 per decile × decile (0.0001–0.0008): each decile of the adoptive-home index added about 0.15 percentage points of risk at the lowest decile of the biological-relative index and about 0.6 at the highest (editors' calculation on the study card). No heritability estimated. As summarized by Prom-Wormley et al. (2017): polygenic scores explained less than 1% of the variance in alcohol dependence; no twin heritability figure for any drug use disorder is given.

statement: In one pre-registered online experiment with adults who had no personal or close-family history of substance use or psychiatric diagnoses, the words used to describe a person's difficulty changed some of the attitudes readers reported, but not others, and did not reliably change a pretend money task. 1,613 adults (largest age group 18 to 25; 55.9% women; 77.1% White; recruited through a university participation scheme, Prolific and social media; country of residence not stated) were each randomly assigned to read one short story about a person called Alex. When Alex's serious trouble at home and work was said to come from increasing drug use rather than from a health concern (819 against 741 readers), readers reported wanting more social distance from Alex (standardized difference d 0.87), saw Alex as more dangerous (d 0.78) and gave higher public-stigma scores (d 0.95; means 50.6 against 42.2), large differences by the usual standard; they agreed less that the condition had genetic or disease causes (d −0.35), and their hope for Alex's recovery was the same within the study's equivalence bounds (d −0.06). Among readers of the drug-use story, calling the condition a 'chronically relapsing brain disease' rather than a 'problem' (392 against 423) made readers agree more that it had genetic or disease causes (d 0.54; the study calls this subscale blame), while its effects on social distance (d −0.20), danger (−0.11), hope (−0.07) and public stigma (−0.18) were small and inconclusive, so the study could not tell whether they were more than trivial; on the means, the brain-disease label went with slightly less social distance and public stigma. In a pretend task in which readers could give or take small sums of money for Alex's answers, neither the drug-use description nor the brain-disease label reliably changed what they gave or took, and describing Alex's treatment as likely to succeed rather than uncertain gave only inconclusive differences (Pennington et al., 2023). The study measured attitudes reported after one made-up story, not how people who use drugs are actually treated by the public, health workers or services; it left out people with lived experience; in the drug-use version four questionnaire items named opioids, so that comparison changed the questions as well as the story; the intervals printed as 99% match 98% intervals; and it did not compare person-first words with labels for the person. Kelly & Westerhoff (2010), a randomized study of two commonly used terms for people with substance-related conditions, is not yet read. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: Do the words used about people who use drugs change how others see them? In one experiment, 1,613 adults online each read one short story about a person called Alex, with the wording chosen at random. When Alex's trouble was said to come from drug use rather than a health concern, readers wanted to keep more distance from Alex, saw Alex as more dangerous and gave higher stigma scores, by a lot. Calling it a 'brain disease' instead of a 'problem' made readers think more that it came from genes or illness, but its other effects were too small to be sure of. Neither wording clearly changed how much pretend money readers gave Alex or took away. Readers rated a made-up story, people who had used drugs themselves were left out, and the study did not test person-first words.
population: Adults recruited online (university participation scheme, Prolific, social media; country of residence not stated; largest age group 18–25) without their own or a close relative's substance use or psychiatric diagnosis; 1,613 randomized
exposure: Reading a short story in which a person's difficulty was described as drug use (against a health concern); within the drug-use story, as a 'chronically relapsing brain disease' (against a 'problem'); and treatment framed as likely to succeed (against uncertain)
comparator: Readers randomly assigned to the other wording
outcome: Self-reported social distance, perceived danger, hope for recovery, genetic or disease attribution (the study's blame subscale), need for continued care and public stigma; rewards and punishments in a pretend money task
magnitude: Pennington et al. (2023), Cohen's d with intervals printed as 99% that match 98% intervals (card reporting issue): drug use vs health concern (819 vs 741): social distance 0.87 (0.74 to 0.99), perceived danger 0.78 (0.66 to 0.90), public stigma 0.95 (0.82 to 1.07; means 50.59 vs 42.15), blame subscale (genetic or disease attribution) −0.35 (−0.47 to −0.23), all meaningful by the study's rule; prognostic optimism −0.06 (equivalent); continued care 0.09 (inconclusive); reward −0.03 (equivalent; 248.11 vs 249.72 pence); punishment 0.14 (0.02 to 0.26; inconclusive). 'Chronically relapsing brain disease' vs 'problem' (392 vs 423, drug-use arm): blame subscale 0.54 (0.38 to 0.71; means 8.61 vs 7.22), meaningful; continued care 0.01 (equivalent); social distance −0.20 (−0.36 to −0.03), prognostic optimism −0.07, danger −0.11, public stigma −0.18 (−0.34 to −0.02; means 49.62 vs 51.20) and reward 0.15, all inconclusive; punishment 0.007 (equivalent). Treatment framed as likely to succeed vs uncertain (383 vs 362): every self-report measure and reward inconclusive (for example public stigma 0.31, 0.14 to 0.48, higher with the uncertain framing), punishment equivalent. Detectable equivalence bounds ±0.28 and ±0.30 for the label and treatment comparisons.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2, some concerns (card sc_pennington_2023): people who failed a manipulation check were left out of that analysis (3.3% to 12%, not given by condition); attitudes reported right after an explicit story are open to demand effects; for the drug-use against health-concern comparison the questionnaire wording also differed (four items named opioids).

inconsistency.note: One study; earlier vignette studies, as the paper describes them, also found drug problems more stigmatized than other conditions but disagree on the brain-disease label, partly because they used different measures.

indirectness.note: A young online convenience sample without lived experience, one hypothetical story, and self-reported attitudes and a pretend money task instead of how people who use drugs are treated; the words tested describe the condition, not the person, so person-first wording was not tested.

imprecision.note: The drug-use contrasts are precise (for example d 0.87, 0.74 to 0.99); the label effects that are inconclusive are stated as such, not as no effect.

publication_bias.note: Registered report accepted before the results; all outcomes reported.

grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high; down one for risk of bias and one for indirectness: low. The verb increases rests on random assignment within the experiment; the rating concerns how far the result carries to other people, other words and real treatment. The intervals printed as 99% match 98% intervals and one p value is printed as below .01 when it is about .011 (card reporting issues); the study's classifications do not change. Kelly & Westerhoff (2010), the randomized study of terms for the person, is not yet read and could add the person-first comparison this study lacks. Status single study.
